Key Points

Interested in Constellation Software Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

Revenue rose 19% to $3.5 billion, with organic growth of 2%. Recurring revenue grew organically by 4%, offset by declines in license revenue (17%) and professional services (5%).

U.S. healthcare businesses declined about 10%, weighed down largely by acquired businesses that were expected to shrink. Excluding two recent acquisitions, the group would have declined about 3%.

Cash from operations increased 5% to $717 million, while shareholder free cash flow fell 16% to $443 million, largely due to a $117 million noncash revaluation charge. Without the charge increasing from last year, free cash flow would have risen about 3%.

This Tech ETF Is Beating QQQ—and Canada May Be Part of the Reason

Constellation Software (TSE:CSU) reported third-quarter revenue of $3.5 billion, up 19%, as growth in recurring revenue was partly offset by declines in licenses and professional services.

Overall organic growth was 2%, while maintenance and other recurring revenue grew organically by 4%, President and Chief Operating Officer Mark Miller said on the company's 2026 third-quarter earnings call. License revenue fell 17% and professional services revenue declined 5%, with both figures subject to quarter-to-quarter fluctuations, he said.

→ Airbnb Defied a Brutal Tech Sell-Off, But Can Its Post-Earnings Rally Last?

Miller described recurring revenue as an important indicator of how customers continue to use Constellation's systems. Excluding U.S. healthcare businesses, particularly Altera, maintenance and recurring revenue would have grown by about 5%, he said.

Healthcare Declines Weigh on Growth

Constellation's U.S. healthcare businesses were down about 10% in the quarter, compared with a 1% decline in the previous quarter, Miller said. Much of the deterioration came from recently acquired businesses that Constellation expected to shrink when it bought them, he added.

→ IonQ's Record Revenue Includes a Big SkyWater Boost: Does That Change the Story?

Excluding two recently acquired businesses, the healthcare group would have been down about 3%, according to Miller. He said the anticipated declines were included in the company's investment assessments and that the healthcare investments discussed on the call were expected to meet their underwritten internal rate of return targets.

Chief Financial Officer Jamal Baksh said the U.S. healthcare group comprises roughly 50 small businesses and that the circumstances at Altera should not be generalized across the entire group. He characterized healthcare as a difficult market because of consolidation.

title: Beyond the Election: 4 ETFs I'm Continuing to Buy No Matter What the Market Does in 2027
detail:
Beyond the Election: 4 ETFs I'm Continuing to Buy No Matter What the Market Does in 2027
David Dierking, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 8:05 AM CST 5 min read
QQQ
VOO
^NDX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The Invesco QQQ ETF, which tracks the Nasdaq 100 index, is down more than 13% from its October high. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is holding up modestly better, only down about 6% from its high. Much of this decline has happened since the U.S. midterm election, where Democrats won races across the country and will be in the majority in both the House and the Senate.

This past week will test investors' stomachs and whether they view the current stretch as an opportunity to buy the dip or a reason to run for the exits. Short-term volatility can feel painful and make your brokerage account look even worse. But if you're a long-term investor, this should be viewed as a normal bump in the road that can be taken advantage of.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That's why I'd still look at buying four ETFs for 2027 and beyond.

Source: Getty Images.
1. Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF

If you're still building up the core of your portfolio or want to establish a foundational position, the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (NYSEMKT: VTI) remains one of the best choices for U.S. equity exposure. It goes beyond just the S&P 500 to include mid-cap and small-cap stocks, two groups that have been outperforming large-caps in 2026.

In my opinion, there's never really a bad time to add the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF or the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF to your portfolio as long-term holdings. The current election volatility, however, allows you to pick up shares at a 6% discount and bump up your returns once stocks recover.

2. Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF

When the market begins to look uncertain, quality matters. It's the one factor that investors tend to gravitate toward in search of safety. The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSEMKT: SCHD) does it better than perhaps any other ETF. It looks at several balance sheet fundamental metrics to select quality dividend-paying stocks, helping to ensure the fund is a portfolio built to withstand a potential downturn.

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF has staged an impressive rebound in 2026 following three years of disappointing returns. It's clearly been helped by its overweight in energy stocks, but the overall diversity of sector holdings -- big overweights in consumer staples and healthcare -- helps ease tech reliance in your portfolio and add some defensive posturing should the markets continue to correct.
